claim: Primate evolution has led to a remarkable diversity of behavioral specializations among species.
source: Primate evolution has led to a remarkable diversity of behavioral specializations and pronounced brain size variation among species (Barton, 2012; DeCasien and Higham, 2019; Powell et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barton 2012, DeCasien and Higham 2019, and Powell et al. 2017

claim: Primate evolution has led to pronounced brain size variation among species.
source: Primate evolution has led to a remarkable diversity of behavioral specializations and pronounced brain size variation among species (Barton, 2012; DeCasien and Higham, 2019; Powell et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barton 2012, DeCasien and Higham 2019, and Powell et al. 2017

claim: Gene expression has been explored in very few primate species to date.
source: Gene expression provides a promising opportunity for studying the molecular basis of brain evolution, but it has been explored in very few primate species to date (e.g. Khaitovich et al., 2005; Khrameeva et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2022; Somel et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Khaitovich et al. 2005, Khrameeva et al. 2020, Ma et al. 2022, Somel et al. 2009)

claim: The study generated and analyzed RNA-seq data from four brain regions in eighteen primate species.
source: To understand the landscape of gene expression evolution across the primate lineage, we generated and analyzed RNA-seq data from four brain regions in an unprecedented eighteen species.
evidence: Direct statement of the study's methodology and sample size

claim: There is a remarkable level of variation in gene expression among hominid species, including humans and chimpanzees.
source: Here, we show a remarkable level of variation in gene expression among hominid species, including humans and chimpanzees, despite their relatively recent divergence time from other primates.
evidence: Supported by the study's RNA-seq data analysis

claim: Individual genes display a wide range of expression dynamics across evolutionary time.
source: We found that individual genes display a wide range of expression dynamics across evolutionary time reflective of the diverse selection pressures acting on genes within primate brain tissue.
evidence: Supported by the study's analysis of gene expression patterns

claim: The study samples represent a 190-fold difference in primate brain size.
source: Using our samples that represent a 190-fold difference in primate brain size, we identified genes with variation in expression most correlated with brain size.
evidence: Direct statement about the range of brain sizes in the sample

claim: Primates are distinguished from other mammals by their large brains relative to body size.
source: Primates are distinguished from other mammals by their large brains relative to body size (Boddy et al., 2012; Martin, 1981; Smaers et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boddy et al. 2012, Martin 1981, and Smaers et al. 2021

claim: There is remarkable variation in behavioral specializations among primate species, including differences in social structure, spatial, dietary and visual ecology, and locomotion.
source: Among the diversity of primate species, there is remarkable variation in behavioral specializations, including differences in social structure, spatial, dietary and visual ecology, and locomotion (Powell et al., 2017; Barton, 2012; DeCasien and Higham, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Powell et al. 2017, Barton 2012, and DeCasien and Higham 2019

claim: Humans possess exceptionally large brains.
source: Humans are unmatched in possessing exceptionally large brains and unparalleled cognitive abilities, such as language (Konopka and Roberts, 2016; Rilling, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Konopka and Roberts 2016 and Rilling 2014

claim: Humans possess unparalleled cognitive abilities, such as language.
source: Humans are unmatched in possessing exceptionally large brains and unparalleled cognitive abilities, such as language (Konopka and Roberts, 2016; Rilling, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Konopka and Roberts 2016 and Rilling 2014

claim: King and Wilson (1975) proposed that the basis of physical and behavioral phenotypic differences between humans and chimpanzees must be found in changes within gene regulatory regions that drive expression.
source: Upon observing the remarkable similarity between human and chimpanzee protein sequences, King and Wilson, 1975 proposed that the basis of the physical and behavioral phenotypic differences between these two species must be found in changes within gene regulatory regions that drive expression.
evidence: Direct citation to King and Wilson 1975

claim: Previous studies on gene expression in primate brain tissues have mostly focused on the neocortex and cerebellum in human, chimpanzee, and rhesus macaque.
source: In studies focusing on gene expression in primate brain tissues, research has mostly focused on the neocortex and cerebellum in human, chimpanzee, and rhesus macaque (Babbitt et al., 2010; Blekhman et al., 2010; Khaitovich et al., 2005; Khaitovich et al., 2004; Khrameeva et al., 2020; Konopka et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2022; Somel et al., 2009; Sousa et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: The study sampled prefrontal cortex, primary visual cortex, hippocampus, and lateral cerebellum from 18 primate species.
source: In the current study, we sampled prefrontal cortex (PFC), primary visual cortex (V1), hippocampus (HIP), and lateral cerebellum (CBL) from 18 primate species, the broadest diversity of primates sampled in any study of gene expression in the brain to date, including species from several rarely-studied lineages.
evidence: Direct statement of the study's sampling methodology

claim: This study represents the broadest diversity of primates sampled in any study of gene expression in the brain to date.
source: In the current study, we sampled prefrontal cortex (PFC), primary visual cortex (V1), hippocampus (HIP), and lateral cerebellum (CBL) from 18 primate species, the broadest diversity of primates sampled in any study of gene expression in the brain to date, including species from several rarely-studied lineages.
evidence: Direct statement comparing this study to previous work

claim: The dataset represents 70–90 million years of primate evolution.
source: Our dataset represents 70–90 million years (Perelman et al., 2011) of primate evolution, providing a more thorough understanding of the evolution of gene expression across primates and allowing for an unprecedented view of how gene expression in the brain has changed over time across all major clades of primate phylogeny.
evidence: Supported by citation to Perelman et al. 2011 for evolutionary timescale

claim: The study generated RNA-seq data from 18 primate species including five hominoids, four cercopithecoids, four platyrrhines, and five strepsirrhines, with 1–3 biological replicates.
source: To understand how gene expression in the brain has evolved across the primate lineage, we generated and analyzed RNA-seq data from 18 primate species (including five hominoids, four cercopithecoids, four platyrrhines, and five strepsirrhines, with 1–3 biological replicates) across four brain regions, including PFC, V1, HIP, and CBL (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Direct statement of the study's sample composition

claim: The study quantified the expression of 15,017 orthologs within hominoids.
source: We quantified the expression of 15,017 orthologs within hominoids, and 3432 on-to-one orthologs across all 18 species (Supplementary files 2 and 3).
evidence: Direct statement of the number of orthologs analyzed

claim: The study quantified the expression of 3432 one-to-one orthologs across all 18 species.
source: We quantified the expression of 15,017 orthologs within hominoids, and 3432 on-to-one orthologs across all 18 species (Supplementary files 2 and 3).
evidence: Direct statement of the number of orthologs analyzed

claim: Variation in interspecific mammalian gene expression has been shown to be less pronounced than that observed across samples from different organs.
source: Variation in interspecific mammalian gene expression has been shown to be less pronounced than that observed across samples from different organs, reflecting the diversity of underlying organ physiology (Brawand et al., 2011; Sudmant et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brawand et al. 2011 and Sudmant et al. 2015

claim: The rate of gene expression divergence evolved more slowly within the cerebral cortex and cerebellum compared to other organ systems from developmentally distinct germ layers.
source: Furthermore, it has been reported that the rate of gene expression divergence evolved more slowly within the cerebral cortex and cerebellum compared to other organ systems from developmentally distinct germ layers (Brawand et al., 2011; Khaitovich et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brawand et al. 2011 and Khaitovich et al. 2005

claim: The 500 most variable protein-coding genes were enriched with glycoproteins, signal peptides, and plasma membrane proteins, with roles in immune function, molecular trafficking, and cell signaling.
source: This subset of genes was enriched with glycoproteins, signal peptides, and plasma membrane proteins, with roles in immune function, molecular trafficking, and cell signaling.
evidence: Supported by the study's enrichment analysis of the most variable genes

claim: Taxon assignment explains a large amount of variation in the dataset, with clear trends emerging independent of brain region.
source: As predicted, taxon assignment explains a large amount of variation to the dataset, with clear trends emerging independent of brain region.
evidence: Supported by the PCoA analysis results

claim: The greatest divergence in expression patterns is observed among hominoid and strepsirrhine species.
source: We find the greatest divergence in expression patterns among hominoid and strepsirrhine species, while there is more similarity observed among cercopithecoids and platyrrhines.
evidence: Supported by the PCoA analysis results

claim: More similarity in expression patterns is observed among cercopithecoids and platyrrhines.
source: We find the greatest divergence in expression patterns among hominoid and strepsirrhine species, while there is more similarity observed among cercopithecoids and platyrrhines.
evidence: Supported by the PCoA analysis results

claim: Hominoids display the greatest level of diversity of any primate phylogenetic group.
source: The hominoids, displaying the greatest level of diversity of any primate phylogenetic group, demonstrate variation that is particularly apparent along Axis 1 and largely driven by human and chimpanzee expression patterns (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by the PCoA analysis and Figure 2A, B

claim: Hominoid variation in gene expression is largely driven by human and chimpanzee expression patterns.
source: The hominoids, displaying the greatest level of diversity of any primate phylogenetic group, demonstrate variation that is particularly apparent along Axis 1 and largely driven by human and chimpanzee expression patterns (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by the PCoA analysis and Figure 2A, B

claim: Hominoids display more variation than strepsirrhines by about 24%.
source: When Axis 1 and 2 of the PCoA are plotted on the same bivariate plot (Figure 2a), the hominoids display more variation than the strepsirrhines by about 24% (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of PCoA data shown in Figure 2a and Supplementary file 5

claim: A large portion of the variation in strepsirrhines is attributed to evolutionary divergence over about 63 million years.
source: However, a large portion of the variation in the strepsirrhines is attributed to evolutionary divergence over about 63 million years (since the last common ancestor of lemurs and lorises), whereas the variation within hominoids has largely accrued over only 9 million years (since humans and chimpanzees shared an ancestor with gorillas).
evidence: Based on known evolutionary timescales

claim: The variation within hominoids has largely accrued over only 9 million years.
source: However, a large portion of the variation in the strepsirrhines is attributed to evolutionary divergence over about 63 million years (since the last common ancestor of lemurs and lorises), whereas the variation within hominoids has largely accrued over only 9 million years (since humans and chimpanzees shared an ancestor with gorillas).
evidence: Based on known evolutionary timescales

claim: Hominoids show remarkable variation despite representing a much shorter evolutionary divergence time compared to strepsirrhines.
source: Therefore, a remarkable finding of this analysis is how much variation is represented by hominoids, despite the fact that this lineage represents a much shorter evolutionary divergence time.
evidence: Inference from the comparison of variation and divergence times

claim: The variation attributed to the cerebellum is distinguished from that of prefrontal cortex, primary visual cortex, and hippocampus.
source: Here, we observe that the variation attributed to CBL is distinguished from that of PFC, V1, and HIP, which are very similar in their distributions.
evidence: Supported by the PCoA analysis results

claim: The cerebellum develops from a different part of the embryonic neural tube (the hindbrain) compared to other sampled brain regions (forebrain).
source: The fact that CBL differs in its pattern of gene expression from other brain regions (Hawrylycz et al., 2015; Hawrylycz et al., 2012; Itõ, 2012) is not surprising given that it is the only sampled region that develops from a different part of the embryonic neural tube (namely, the hindbrain vs. forebrain) and exhibits a neuronal packing density (predominantly glutamatergic granule cells) that far exceeds these other brain regions (Azevedo et al., 2009; Herculano-Houzel, 2011; Itō, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to developmental neuroscience literature

claim: The cerebellum exhibits a neuronal packing density that far exceeds other sampled brain regions.
source: The fact that CBL differs in its pattern of gene expression from other brain regions (Hawrylycz et al., 2015; Hawrylycz et al., 2012; Itõ, 2012) is not surprising given that it is the only sampled region that develops from a different part of the embryonic neural tube (namely, the hindbrain vs. forebrain) and exhibits a neuronal packing density (predominantly glutamatergic granule cells) that far exceeds these other brain regions (Azevedo et al., 2009; Herculano-Houzel, 2011; Itō, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Azevedo et al. 2009, Herculano-Houzel 2011, and Itō 2012

claim: Enrichments for cerebellar gene expression reveal expression changes to categories such as 'Cell Surface Receptor Signaling Pathway,' 'Cell Projection Organization,' and 'Wnt Signaling Pathway.'
source: Enrichments for cerebellar gene expression reveal expression changes to categories such as 'Cell Surface Receptor Signaling Pathway,' 'Cell Projection Organization,' and 'Wnt Signaling Pathway.'
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis

claim: The cerebellum shows a unique increase in signaling activity-related terms compared to other brain regions.
source: Although all the brain regions surveyed show some enrichment for categories related to cell signaling, the cerebellum shows a unique increase in signaling activity-related terms (both in the number of enrichment categories and the degree of change associated with these categories).
evidence: Supported by comparative enrichment analysis across brain regions

claim: Samples derived from individuals of the same species tended to be grouped together in expression phenograms, regardless of brain region.
source: Samples that were derived from individuals of the same species tended to be grouped together, regardless of brain region, revealing that inter-individual differences are minor compared to other sources of variation.
evidence: Supported by the phenogram analysis results

claim: Inter-individual differences in gene expression are minor compared to other sources of variation.
source: Samples that were derived from individuals of the same species tended to be grouped together, regardless of brain region, revealing that inter-individual differences are minor compared to other sources of variation.
evidence: Inference from the phenogram clustering patterns

claim: Gene expression profiles replicated the phylogenetic relationships of closely related species when all regions were considered.
source: Gene expression profiles also replicated the phylogenetic relationships of closely related species (e.g. humans and chimpanzees; pig-tailed and rhesus macaques) when all regions were considered, but these relationships became less phylogenetically structured in the phenograms constructed using expression data from individual brain regions.
evidence: Supported by the phenogram analysis results

claim: All neighbor-joining phenograms accurately represent cercopithecoids and strepsirrhines as monophyletic groups.
source: All neighbor-joining phenograms accurately represent cercopithecoids and strepsirrhines as monophyletic groups; however, expression data produces paraphyletic groups of hominoid and platyrrhine species.
evidence: Supported by the phenogram analysis results

claim: Expression data produces paraphyletic groups of hominoid and platyrrhine species.
source: All neighbor-joining phenograms accurately represent cercopithecoids and strepsirrhines as monophyletic groups; however, expression data produces paraphyletic groups of hominoid and platyrrhine species.
evidence: Supported by the phenogram analysis results

claim: Taxa with longer periods of independent evolution are more likely to show divergent patterns of gene expression than more closely related groups.
source: This result potentially reflects the fact that taxa with longer periods of independent evolution (i.e. strepsirrhines) are more likely to show divergent patterns of gene expression than more closely related groups.
evidence: Inference from the phenogram results

claim: Models that incorporate stabilizing selection are more accurately able to predict gene expression evolution in mammals than models that account only for neutral drift.
source: Previous studies have shown how models that incorporate stabilizing selection are more accurately able to predict gene expression evolution in mammals than models that account only for neutral drift (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al. 2019

claim: Approximately 15–20% of genes show differential expression across all species-to-species comparisons.
source: Across all expressed one-to-one orthologs represented in the sampled primates, we found that ~15–20% of genes show differential expression across all species-to-species comparisons (q-value <0.05).
evidence: Supported by the differential expression analysis results

claim: The relative amount of differential expression increases over evolutionary time, both between species and clades.
source: As expected, the relative amount of differential expression increases over evolutionary time, both between species and clades (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 ).
evidence: Supported by the differential expression analysis and Figure 3

claim: Species and clade-wise comparisons show larger numbers of differentially expressed genes when strepsirrhines are included in the contrast.
source: However, both the species and clade-wise comparisons show larger numbers of differentially expressed (DE) genes in the comparisons when strepsirrhines are included in the contrast, a result of the more than 60 million years of independent evolution of this taxon.
evidence: Supported by the differential expression analysis results

claim: In the cerebellum, the lemur, baboon, and human samples show relatively higher levels of differential expression compared to other species.
source: In the cerebellum, the lemur, baboon, and human samples are particularly unique and show relatively higher levels of DE compared to other species.
evidence: Supported by the UpSet plot analysis

claim: In the hippocampus, visual cortex, and prefrontal cortex, chimpanzees show higher differential expression than human samples.
source: However, in the hippocampus, visual cortex, and prefrontal cortex, the chimpanzees appear to show higher DE than the human samples.
evidence: Supported by the UpSet plot analysis

claim: The cerebellum is a particularly unique brain structure in terms of gene expression patterns.
source: This suggests again that the cerebellum is a particularly unique brain structure and that chimpanzee gene expression is significantly different in the other three brain regions studied, warranting further analysis.
evidence: Inference from the differential expression patterns

claim: Human prefrontal cortex shows an enrichment of metabolic processes when compared to other primates.
source: When comparing gene expression in the PFC of humans relative to other primates, human PFC shows an enrichment of metabolic processes, including 'regulation of cellular metabolic process' and 'regulation of macromolecule metabolic process' (Supplementary files 6 and 7).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis

claim: Comparing human and chimpanzee prefrontal cortex reveals that categories supporting neural growth and development are enriched as differentially expressed in human PFC relative to chimpanzees.
source: Comparing human and chimpanzee PFC reveals that categories that support neural growth and development (e.g. 'neuron projection morphogenesis,' 'cell morphogenesis involved in neuron differentiation'), gene regulation, and metabolic processes are enriched as differentially expressed in human PFC relative to chimpanzees.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis

claim: APP (amyloid precursor protein) appears to be upregulated in humans compared to siamang under the category of 'Positive Regulation of Transcription by RNA polymerase II'.
source: Of interest, under the category of 'Positive Regulation of Transcription by RNA polymerase II' we find several genes that appear to be upregulated in humans compared to siamang: APP (amyloid precursor protein, related to plaque formation in Alzheimer's disease) as well as PRKN (found to be causal in Parkinson's disease) (Funayama et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis

claim: PRKN appears to be upregulated in humans compared to siamang under the category of 'Positive Regulation of Transcription by RNA polymerase II'.
source: Of interest, under the category of 'Positive Regulation of Transcription by RNA polymerase II' we find several genes that appear to be upregulated in humans compared to siamang: APP (amyloid precursor protein, related to plaque formation in Alzheimer's disease) as well as PRKN (found to be causal in Parkinson's disease) (Funayama et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis and citation to Funayama et al. 2023

claim: When examining Hominini compared to other Great Apes, terms related to 'Regulation of Metabolic Process,' 'Nervous System Development,' and 'Biosynthetic processes' are all enriched within the hippocampus.
source: When examining Hominini (humans and chimpanzees) compared to other Great Apes, terms related to 'Regulation of Metabolic Process,' 'Nervous System Development,' and 'Biosynthetic processes' are all enriched within the hippocampus.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis

claim: 'Negative Regulation of Synaptic Transmission' was enriched in other ape species compared to Hominini.
source: Meanwhile, 'Negative Regulation of Synaptic Transmission' was enriched in the other ape species.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis

claim: There is a general trend of decreasing specificity in enrichment categories over increasing evolutionary time among various species and clade comparisons.
source: Overall, among various species and clade comparisons, there is a general trend of decreasing specificity in enrichment categories over increasing evolutionary time.
evidence: Inference from comparative enrichment analysis across evolutionary distances

claim: Gene expression in brain regions sampled from the lorises diverged from other strepsirrhines and other primates more generally.
source: Our PCoA analyses showed that gene expression in brain regions sampled from the lorises (i.e. the slender loris, slow loris, and pygmy slow loris) diverged from other strepsirrhines, and other primates more generally (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by PCoA analysis and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Individual genes exhibit wide variation in expression dynamics across the primate lineage.
source: Using the OU model, we found that individual genes exhibit wide variation in expression dynamics across the primate lineage (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by OU model analysis and Figure 4a

claim: Genes showing low variation or stabilizing selection are enriched for categories related to transport and cellular localization.
source: Enrichments for genes showing low variation or stabilizing selection (q=0.05) reveal categories related to transport and cellular localization (GO Biological Processes, Supplementary files 6 and 7).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis

claim: Genes that are less constrained or neutrally evolving have processes related to neuron morphogenesis, plasticity, and cell death.
source: In contrast, genes that are less constrained or neutrally evolving (q>0.05) have a number of processes related to neuron morphogenesis, plasticity, and cell death.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis

claim: Pairwise expression differences between humans and other species increasingly diverge with evolutionary distance in all brain regions sampled.
source: Here, we find that pairwise expression differences between humans and the other species increasingly diverge with evolutionary distance in all brain regions sampled (Figure 4b); however, these pairwise comparisons do not seem to saturate with evolutionary time across the primate comparisons (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by analysis of pairwise expression differences and Figure 4b

claim: Pairwise expression comparisons do not saturate with evolutionary time across the primate comparisons.
source: Here, we find that pairwise expression differences between humans and the other species increasingly diverge with evolutionary distance in all brain regions sampled (Figure 4b); however, these pairwise comparisons do not seem to saturate with evolutionary time across the primate comparisons (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by analysis of pairwise expression differences and Figure 4b

claim: Across tissues, on average, 64% of genes fit better under stabilizing selection.
source: In this analysis, we found that across tissues, on average, 64% of genes fit better under stabilizing selection (64% CBL, 59% HIP, 72% PFC, and 60% V1; FDR-corrected q-value calculated via the BH procedure to correct for multiple hypothesis testing; FDR threshold of 5% to determine significance).
evidence: Supported by EVEE-tools analysis using the OU model

claim: The overall phylogenetic signal in brain expression divergence using the OU model was slightly smaller than observed with edgeR.
source: In the context of the OU model of continuous trait evolution, we found that the overall phylogenetic signal in brain expression divergence was slightly smaller than observed with edgeR over the entire combined dataset (EVEE: 4–6.7% across all single species comparisons using a logFC of +/-2; edgeR: 15–20%).
evidence: Comparison of results from two different analytical methods

claim: The relative amount of differential expression increases gradually with evolutionary distance.
source: However, the relative amount of differential expression does increase gradually with evolutionary distance (as expected based on results in edgeR).
evidence: Supported by EVEE-tools analysis

claim: The human and chimpanzee comparison shows considerable variation in differential expression across the four brain regions.
source: The only exception to this is the human and chimpanzee comparison, which shows considerable variation in differential expression across the four brain regions.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis

claim: The increase in differential expression between humans and chimpanzees suggests directional selection within that lineage.
source: Representing such a short period of evolutionary divergence, this increase in DE suggests direction selection within that lineage.
evidence: Inference from the pattern of differential expression relative to divergence time

claim: A significant FDR (<5%) was not reached in the outlier expression dataset among all species comparisons.
source: It is important to note that a significant FDR (<5%) was not reached in this dataset, among all species comparisons.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical significance

claim: A mammalian dataset was unable to reach an FDR below 18% in previous applications of the EVEE package.
source: This is expected based on previous applications of this package, in which a mammalian dataset was also unable to reach an FDR below 18% (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al. 2019

claim: Patterns of outlier gene expression occur in a species and tissue-specific manner.
source: In our outlier expression analysis, we found that patterns of outlier gene expression occur in a species and tissue-specific manner (Supplementary file 10).
evidence: Supported by outlier expression analysis

claim: In the prefrontal cortex, the chimpanzee and marmoset samples have the highest number of outlier genes deviating from average expression patterns.
source: For example, in the PFC, the chimpanzee and marmoset samples appear to have the highest number of outlier genes deviating from average expression patterns (compared to human, siamang, baboon, rhesus macaque, and marmoset samples).
evidence: Supported by outlier expression analysis

claim: Outlier analysis in the cerebellum reveals that the human and lemur samples have the highest number of outlier genes.
source: In contrast to the PFC, outlier analysis in the CBL reveals that the human and lemur samples have the highest number of outlier genes.
evidence: Supported by outlier expression analysis

claim: Many outlier genes are related to functions in development, transcription, nervous system development, neurogenesis, and metabolism.
source: Upon gene set category enrichment analysis, we find that many of these genes that are deemed 'outliers' are related to functions in development, transcription, nervous system development, neurogenesis, and metabolism.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of outlier genes

claim: The chimpanzee prefrontal cortex shows a significant upregulation in genes involved in energy storage and transfer, such as ETFA and NDUFS4.
source: For example, the chimpanzee PFC shows a significant upregulation in genes involved in energy storage and transfer, such as ETFA and NDUFS4, which are both involved in electron transport for ATP generation, as well as ANKH, implicated in phosphate transport (Szeri et al., 2020; Henriques et al., 2021; Shil et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis and citations

claim: The chimpanzee prefrontal cortex shows unique expression patterns in genes related to synaptic activity and neurotransmitter release, including significant downregulation of GABRA4 and SYN1.
source: We also see that the chimpanzee PFC shows unique expression patterns in genes related to synaptic activity and neurotransmitter release, including significant downregulation of GABRA4 and SYN1 (Fassio et al., 2011; Fan et al., 2020 Fan et al., 2020; Fassio et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis and citations

claim: The human cerebellum and prefrontal cortex both display a significant upregulation of genes related to Amyloid protein production (APP).
source: In contrast, the human CBL and PFC both display a significant upregulation of genes related to Amyloid protein production (APP), a major component of many neurodegenerative diseases with functions in synaptic signaling (O'Brien and Wong, 2011).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis and citation to O'Brien and Wong 2011

claim: The human cerebellum shows enrichments in genes related to neurogenesis and synaptic activity, including SDK1, FZD5, and CDH10.
source: Unique to the human CBL we also see enrichments in genes related to neurogenesis and synaptic activity, including SDK1, FZD5, and CDH10 (Redies et al., 2012; Slater et al., 2013; Bagot et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis and citations

claim: The percentage of genes that fit better under the model of stabilizing selection is not statistically different when using different reference species (human, siamang, or rhesus macaque).
source: The percentage of genes that fit better under the model of stabilizing selection (in comparison to neutral drift) is not statistically different from those observed when using humans as a reference (on average, 58–64% across all four major brain regions).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis using different reference species

claim: The effects of the reference species used for normalization are negligible in terms of analyzing differential expression across the primate tree.
source: We additionally looked at pairwise species comparisons to determine if the general trends of directional selection and differential gene expression were comparable to the human-reference data, and again confirmed that the effects of the reference species used for normalization here are negligible in terms of analyzing differential expression across our primate tree.
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis using different reference species

claim: The average brain size across the study species varies by approximately 190 fold.
source: Our dataset provides a unique opportunity to evaluate this question, since the average brain size across our study species varies by ~190 fold.
evidence: Direct statement about the range of brain sizes in the sample

claim: The same genes rank among those with the strongest positive correlation to brain size in prefrontal cortex, primary visual cortex, and hippocampus.
source: Results indicate that the same genes rank among those with the strongest positive correlation in PFC, V1, and HIP.
evidence: Supported by multivariate analysis of gene expression and brain size

claim: The cerebellum includes more variation among the genes most strongly correlated to overall brain size than the other three brain regions.
source: CBL also shares some of these same genes but includes more variation among the genes most strongly correlated to overall brain size than the other three brain regions (Figure 5, Supplementary file 9), potentially reflecting the more recent expansion of the CBL relative to the rest of the neocortex (Miller et al., 2019; Smaers et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multivariate analysis and Figure 5, with citations to Miller et al. 2019 and Smaers et al. 2018

claim: Through more representative sampling of primate species, substantial variation in gene expression levels was found within the hominoid and strepsirrhine lineages.
source: Through more representative sampling of primate species, we found substantial variation in gene expression levels within the hominoid and strepsirrhine lineages, with the diversity among hominoids particularly impressive due to the recent divergence of this taxon.
evidence: Supported by the study's RNA-seq data analysis

claim: Using the OU model, a substantial proportion of genes showed differential expression across species.
source: Using the OU model, we found that a substantial proportion of genes showed differential expression across species.
evidence: Supported by the OU model analysis

claim: The considerable diversity of gene expression in human and chimpanzee brain tissue has profound implications for understanding the distinct evolutionary processes that have acted upon the brains of the ancestral species of these two lineages.
source: The considerable diversity of gene expression in human and chimpanzee brain tissue has profound implications for understanding the distinct evolutionary processes that have acted upon the brains of the ancestral species of these two lineages.
evidence: Inference from the observed diversity in gene expression

claim: Gene expression evolution followed a linear pattern but did not reach a saturation point due to stabilizing selection pressures within Primates.
source: Importantly, gene expression evolution did follow a linear pattern, but did not reach a saturation point due to stabilizing selection pressures as seen in other studies (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by the study's analysis and comparison to Chen et al. 2019

claim: Less constrained, neutrally evolving patterns appeared to be the most prevalent pattern in each brain region studied.
source: Less constrained, neutrally evolving patterns appeared to be the most prevalent pattern in each brain region studied, preventing a saturation point of stabilizing pressures to be reached within Primates with increased phylogenetic distance from humans.
evidence: Supported by the OU model analysis

claim: All samples were obtained from adult individuals free from known neurological disease.
source: All samples were obtained from adult individuals free from known neurological disease.
evidence: Direct statement about sample selection criteria

claim: If available, the right hemisphere was preferentially sampled.
source: If available, the right hemisphere was preferentially sampled.
